newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria oil community crisis spreads eastwards.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria oil community crisis spreads eastwards.

text.p: Nigerian villagers, protesting against a local government election, have occupied a seventh oil installation on the Niger Delta, forcing the Royal Dutch Shell to shut down a total of 10 percent of the nation's oil production.
Shell said on Thursday that Nembe Creek flow station in the east was closed last Saturday and staff withdrawn after the community there told them to stop work.
"The dispute there is connected to the local government election and does not involve us in anyway," a Shell spokesman in Lagos told Reuters.
In all, 210,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil pumped by Shell has been affected.
The dispute in the Nembe area, which affects Bonny light crude stream, is over the amalgamation of two communities into one for the purpose of a recent local government election.
The communities are Ogbolomobiri and Bassambiri, which Nigeria's military government fused to produce one local government council chairman.
They are protesting because the more local governments they have the revenue they will get from the federal purse.
In the Western division, Ijaw tribesmen seized six Shell flow stations last Saturday, detaining 127 staff of the company, all of them Nigerians.
Delicate negotiations have secured the release of most of them, the latest being a batch of 35 ferried by boat on Wednesday night from the Jones Creek flow station.
Shell expects the rest of the hostages to be freed on Thursday and a boat was already on its way to evacuate them from the Egwa flow station, company officials said.
Nigeria's military government, which depends on crude oil exports for more than 90 percent of its foreign exchange income, has not said a word on the disturbances.
The oil communities have long been restive over the lack of modern amenities in their areas despite being the place where Nigeria derives the money that sustains the country.

Mired in political turmoil since 1993 when a presidential election to restore democracy was annulled, Nigeria sank further into crisis in 1995 when nine minority rights campaigners from the oil-producing tribe of Ogoni were hanged.
The nine, including author Ken Saro-Wiwa, had been advocating for a fairer share of oil revenues for the oil-producing states and self-determination for their tribe.
"The Ogoni problem seems to be repeating itelf in other oil areas," said lawyer Enock Fubara, himself an indigene of Rivers state in the Niger delta where much of Nigeria's oil is produced.

"The problem essentially is that we the minorities produce the oil but the proceeds from it go to develop the major tribes in the north, east and west," he said, adding: "It is like a conspiracy of the big tribes against the small ones."
Shell spokesman in Lagos said if the disturbances continued then it was likely the company would call a force majuere soon.
The "force majeure" is a warning by Shell to oil buyers that it will not be able to deliver on contracted oil shipments if the disturbances persist.
"There is a good chance we may not have to do this because we are talking to the communities and are quite hopeful that production could soon restart," he said.
Shell pumps about half Nigeria's daily output of just above two million bpd and the Anglo-Dutch group has had to bear the brunt of the frequent communal problems in the oil areas.
